claim: Mammalian BK-type voltage- and Ca2+-dependent K+ channels are found in a wide range of cells and intracellular organelles.
source: Mammalian BK-type voltage- and Ca2+-dependent K+ channels are found in a wide range of cells and intracellular organelles.
evidence: This is a general statement about BK channel localization presented in the abstract without specific experimental data in this manuscript, but it references established knowledge in the field.

claim: BK channels are expressed in lysosomes with their extracellular side facing the strongly acidified lysosomal lumen (pH ~4.5).
source: For example, it has been reported that BK channels are expressed in lysosomes with their extracellular side facing the strongly acidified lysosomal lumen (pH ~4.5).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature, as indicated by the context of 'it has been reported'.

claim: BK activation is strongly and reversibly inhibited by extracellular H+.
source: Here we show that BK activation is strongly and reversibly inhibited by extracellular H+, with its conductance-voltage relationship shifted by more than +100 mV at pHO 4.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, including current recordings and G-V relationships shown in Figure 1.

claim: The conductance-voltage relationship of BK channels is shifted by more than +100 mV at pHO 4.
source: Here we show that BK activation is strongly and reversibly inhibited by extracellular H+, with its conductance-voltage relationship shifted by more than +100 mV at pHO 4.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by the G-V curve data shown in Figure 1B and 1D.

claim: The inhibition of BK channels by extracellular H+ is mainly caused by H+ inhibition of BK voltage-sensor (VSD) activation.
source: Our results reveal that this inhibition is mainly caused by H+ inhibition of BK voltage-sensor (VSD) activation through three acidic residues on the extracellular side of BK VSD.
evidence: This claim is supported by gating current measurements shown in Figure 3 and mutagenesis data in Figure 5.

claim: Three acidic residues (D133, D147, D153) on the extracellular side of BK VSD are involved in H+ inhibition.
source: Our results reveal that this inhibition is mainly caused by H+ inhibition of BK voltage-sensor (VSD) activation through three acidic residues on the extracellular side of BK VSD. Given that these key residues (D133, D147, D153) are highly conserved among members in the voltage-dependent cation channel superfamily, the mechanism underlying BK inhibition by extracellular acidification might also be applicable to other members in the family.
evidence: This claim is supported by mutagenesis experiments showing that alanine substitutions at these positions reduce pH sensitivity (Figure 5).

claim: The key residues D133, D147, and D153 are highly conserved among members in the voltage-dependent cation channel superfamily.
source: Given that these key residues (D133, D147, D153) are highly conserved among members in the voltage-dependent cation channel superfamily, the mechanism underlying BK inhibition by extracellular acidification might also be applicable to other members in the family.
evidence: This claim is supported by the sequence alignment shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The mechanism underlying BK inhibition by extracellular acidification might also be applicable to other members in the voltage-dependent cation channel superfamily.
source: Given that these key residues (D133, D147, D153) are highly conserved among members in the voltage-dependent cation channel superfamily, the mechanism underlying BK inhibition by extracellular acidification might also be applicable to other members in the family.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the conservation of key residues across channel families.

claim: BK channels are regulated by two distinct physiological signals: Ca2+ and membrane potential.
source: A hallmark of BK-type Ca2+ and voltage-activated K+ channels is its dual regulation by two distinct physiological signals, Ca2+ and membrane potential (Latorre et al., 1982; DiChiara and Reinhart, 1995; Horrigan and Aldrich, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature establishing this fundamental property of BK channels.

claim: The BK channel α subunit contains three linked modules: a pore-gate domain (PGD), a transmembrane voltage-sensor domain (VSD), and two RCK domains forming a cytosolic gating ring (CTD).
source: The key Ca2+ and voltage-sensing functions of the BK channel are embedded within the pore-forming BK α subunit and arise from interactions among three linked modules: a central pore-gate domain (PGD) that forms a K+-selective ion permeation pathway, a transmembrane voltage-sensor domain (VSD) similar to that of the voltage-gate K+ (Kv) channels (Ma et al., 2006), and two regulator of conductance for K+ (RCK) domains that form a cytosolic gating ring (CTD) to provide binding sites for intracellular ligands such as Ca2+ (Schreiber and Salkoff, 1997; Jiang et al., 2001; Shi et al., 2002; Xia et al., 2002, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior structural and functional studies of BK channels.

claim: BK channels exhibit considerable diversity in their functional properties among different loci of expression.
source: Yet, despite the common Ca2+- and voltage-sensing functions of all BK channels, BK channels typically exhibit considerable diversity in their functional properties among different loci of expression, for example, in epithelial cells (Bailey et al., 2006; Grimm et al., 2007), smooth muscle (Robitaille et al., 1993; Wellman and Nelson, 2003; Tanaka et al., 2004), neurons (Reinhart et al., 1991; Rosenblatt et al., 1997; Meredith et al., 2006), potentially even in various organelles (Singh et al., 2013; Li et al., 2014; Cao et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2017), thereby allowing them to play physiological roles suited to their particular location of expression.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies documenting BK channel diversity in different cell types.

claim: Only a single gene (KCa1.1; Kcnma1) encodes the pore-forming subunit of all BK channels.
source: This diversity in function occurs despite the fact that only a single gene (KCa1.1; Kcnma1) encodes the pore-forming subunit of all BK channels.
evidence: This is established knowledge about BK channel genetics.

claim: Diversity in BK channel properties can arise from alternative splicing of pore-forming α subunits.
source: At least some diversity in BK channel properties can arise from the stable cell-specific molecular composition of the BK channel complex, including alternative splicing of pore-forming α subunits (Tseng-Crank et al., 1994; Rosenblatt et al., 1997) and co-assembly with various accessory subunits (Wallner et al., 1996; Xia et al., 1999; Brenner et al., 2000; Xia et al., 2000; Brenner et al., 2005; Yan and Aldrich, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies on BK channel alternative splicing.

claim: Diversity in BK channel properties can arise from co-assembly with various accessory subunits.
source: At least some diversity in BK channel properties can arise from the stable cell-specific molecular composition of the BK channel complex, including alternative splicing of pore-forming α subunits (Tseng-Crank et al., 1994; Rosenblatt et al., 1997) and co-assembly with various accessory subunits (Wallner et al., 1996; Xia et al., 1999; Brenner et al., 2000; Xia et al., 2000; Brenner et al., 2005; Yan and Aldrich, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies on BK channel accessory subunits.

claim: BK channels can be regulated by post-translational modifications such as phosphorylation.
source: BK channels can also be regulated on a shorter time scale by post-translational modifications such as phosphorylation (Tian et al., 2004, 2008) or even more briefly by binding of soluble factors to the BK channel complex, such as Ca2+ (Magleby and Pallotta, 1983; Schreiber and Salkoff, 1997; Xia et al., 2002), Mg2+(Shi and Cui, 2001; Zhang et al., 2001b; Shi et al., 2002; Horrigan and Ma, 2008), heme (Tang et al., 2003; Horrigan et al., 2005), carbon monoxide (Hou et al., 2008b), or omega-3 fatty acid (Hoshi et al., 2013b, 2013a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies on BK channel phosphorylation.

claim: BK channels can be regulated by binding of soluble factors including Ca2+, Mg2+, heme, carbon monoxide, and omega-3 fatty acid.
source: BK channels can also be regulated on a shorter time scale by post-translational modifications such as phosphorylation (Tian et al., 2004, 2008) or even more briefly by binding of soluble factors to the BK channel complex, such as Ca2+ (Magleby and Pallotta, 1983; Schreiber and Salkoff, 1997; Xia et al., 2002), Mg2+(Shi and Cui, 2001; Zhang et al., 2001b; Shi et al., 2002; Horrigan and Ma, 2008), heme (Tang et al., 2003; Horrigan et al., 2005), carbon monoxide (Hou et al., 2008b), or omega-3 fatty acid (Hoshi et al., 2013b, 2013a).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior studies on BK channel regulation by various ligands.

claim: Modulation of BK activity by regulatory factors appears to involve interactions with binding sites on the intracellular side of the BK channel.
source: In the latter cases, modulation of BK activity appears to involve interactions with the regulatory factors to binding sites on the intracellular side of the BK channel.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the cited studies on intracellular BK channel regulation.

claim: Little is known about regulation of BK channels by extracellular soluble factors.
source: In contrast, despite the fact that the extracellular side of BK channels may be exposed to a wide range of microenvironments, little is known about how and even whether regulation of BK channels by extracellular soluble factors may occur.
evidence: This claim reflects the state of knowledge in the field at the time of the study.

claim: Many BK channels are expressed in loci where they may experience extremely low extracellular pH (pHO <5).
source: Many BK channels are expressed in loci where they may experience extremely low extracellular pH (pHO <5).
evidence: This claim is supported by the examples provided in the following sentences about kidney and lysosomes.

claim: BK channels regulate potassium secretion in the distal nephron.
source: For example, BK channels regulate potassium secretion in the distal nephron (Bailey et al., 2006; Grimm et al., 2007), while urinary pH ranges from 6.5 to 7.5 daily in healthy people and may vary from 4.5 to 8.0 in pathological conditions (Wagner et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies on BK channels in the kidney.

claim: Urinary pH ranges from 6.5 to 7.5 daily in healthy people and may vary from 4.5 to 8.0 in pathological conditions.
source: For example, BK channels regulate potassium secretion in the distal nephron (Bailey et al., 2006; Grimm et al., 2007), while urinary pH ranges from 6.5 to 7.5 daily in healthy people and may vary from 4.5 to 8.0 in pathological conditions (Wagner et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature on urinary pH.

claim: BK channels were proposed to regulate Ca2+ release/refilling and membrane trafficking of lysosomes.
source: Recently, BK channels were proposed to regulate Ca2+ release/refilling and membrane trafficking of lysosomes (Cao et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent studies on lysosomal BK channels.

claim: In lysosomes, BK channels are oriented with their extracellular side exposed to high H+ concentration in the lumen.
source: In the case of lysosomes, the BK channels are oriented with their extracellular side exposed to a high concentration of H+ in the lumen of the lysosome, the pH of which ranges from 4.2 to 4.7 (Mindell, 2012; Xu and Ren, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies on lysosomal pH and BK channel orientation.

claim: Lysosomal pH ranges from 4.2 to 4.7.
source: In the case of lysosomes, the BK channels are oriented with their extracellular side exposed to a high concentration of H+ in the lumen of the lysosome, the pH of which ranges from 4.2 to 4.7 (Mindell, 2012; Xu and Ren, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies on lysosomal pH.

claim: Some Kv channels may be sensitive to pHO in the pH range of 5–7.
source: Some previous work on Kv1 (Claydon et al., 2000; Kwan et al., 2006; Claydon et al., 2007, Claydon et al., 2008) and KCNQ channels (Prole et al., 2003) establishes precedence that some Kv channels may be sensitive to pHO in the pH range of 5–7, perhaps by effects on the pore region of these channels (Zhang et al., 2003; Claydon et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies on Kv channel pH sensitivity.

claim: The impact of pHO below pH 5 has not been systematically examined in Kv channels.
source: However, the impact of pHO below pH five such as that which might be found in the lumen of a lysosome has not been systematically examined in Kv channels.
evidence: This claim reflects a gap in the literature that the current study addresses.

claim: The amplitude of macroscopic BK current was reduced at pHO 4, with reduction becoming increasingly apparent as the voltage is made more negative.
source: The amplitude of macroscopic BK current was reduced at pHO 4, with reduction became increasingly apparent as the voltage is made more negative, for example, comparing moderate depolarization at +60 mV (Figure 1A, red traces) to that at +160 mV (Figure 1C, blue trace), or comparing the reduction in inward tails at −120 mV (Figure 1A and B) to the reduction in outward current at +160 mV (Figure 1C, blue trace).
evidence: This claim is supported by the current traces shown in Figure 1A and the analysis in Figure 1B and 1C.

claim: Neutralization of D292 in the BK channel pore region reduces single channel conductance and induces outward rectification.
source: A previous study showed that neutralization of a highly conserved acidic residue (D292N) in the BK channel pore region reduces single channel conductance and induces an outward rectification in resulting BK channels (Haug et al., 2004b).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a prior study on the D292N mutation.

claim: BK single channel conductance was reduced by ~50% at −120 mV and ~20% at +60 mV when pHO was changed from 7 to 4.
source: In a similar fashion, we observed that BK single channel conductance was reduced by ~50% at −120 mV and ~20% at +60 mV when pHO was changed from 7 to 4 (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by single channel conductance measurements shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The reduction of BK single channel conductance induced by extracellular acidification can largely account for the reduction of maximum tail current at −120 mV.
source: This change in single channel conductance can largely account for the reduction of maximum tail current at −120 mV (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of single channel conductance changes with macroscopic current changes.

claim: The reduction of BK single channel conductance accounts for only a small portion of the changes in outward current amplitude over the physiologically relevant voltage range.
source: However, it is also clear that the reduction of BK single channel conductance induced by extracellular acidification accounts for only a small portion of the changes in outward current amplitude over the physiologically relevant voltage range (e.g. the amplitude of macroscopic BK current at +60 mV was reduced by ~85% when pHO was changed from 7 to 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of single channel conductance changes with macroscopic current changes at different voltages.

claim: The amplitude of BK current at pHO 4 evoked by +160 mV pulse was 0.72 ± 0.02 (n = 9) of that at pHO 7.
source: For example, the amplitude of current evoked by +160 mV pulse at pHO 4 was only 0.72 ± 0.02 (n = 9) of that at pHO 7, while the BK single channel conductance at pHO 4 was estimated to be 0.88 of that at pHO 7 at the same voltage (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative measurements from the experiments.

claim: BK single channel conductance at pHO 4 was estimated to be 0.88 of that at pHO 7 at +160 mV.
source: For example, the amplitude of current evoked by +160 mV pulse at pHO 4 was only 0.72 ± 0.02 (n = 9) of that at pHO 7, while the BK single channel conductance at pHO 4 was estimated to be 0.88 of that at pHO 7 at the same voltage (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by single channel conductance measurements and modeling shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Extracellular acidification strongly shifts the voltage-dependent gating of BK channel toward positive potential.
source: Above results indicate that extracellular acidification strongly shifts the voltage-dependent gating of BK channel toward positive potential.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the data showing that conductance changes exceed single channel conductance changes.

claim: The BK half-activation potential (Vh) was shifted by more than +60 mV when pHO was changed from 7 to 5.
source: The BK half-activation potential (Vh) was shifted by more than +60 mV when pHO was changed from 7 to 5 and was further shifted by another +70 mV at pHO 4.
evidence: This claim is supported by the G-V curves and Boltzmann fits shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The BK half-activation potential (Vh) was further shifted by another +70 mV at pHO 4 compared to pHO 5.
source: The BK half-activation potential (Vh) was shifted by more than +60 mV when pHO was changed from 7 to 5 and was further shifted by another +70 mV at pHO 4.
evidence: This claim is supported by the G-V curves and Boltzmann fits shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The PO of BK did not reach maximum level even at +160 mV when pHO was changed from 7 to 4.
source: With a gating shift of this magnitude, the PO of BK did not reach maximum level even at +160 mV when pHO was changed from 7 to 4 (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the G-V curves shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The kinetics of BK current was significantly changed with elevation of extracellular [H+], with activation being much slower while deactivation being much faster at pHO 4 than at pHO 7.
source: In addition to reduction in current amplitude, the kinetics of BK current was also significantly changed with elevation of extracellular [H+], with activation being much slower while deactivation being much faster at pHO 4 than at pHO 7 (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the current traces shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The activation of BK channels remained low over the physiologically relevant voltage range of ±60 mV at pHO 4 even with saturating [Ca2+]in.
source: Importantly, the activation of BK channels remained low over the physiologically relevant voltage range of ±60 mV at pHO 4 even with saturating [Ca2+]in (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the G-V curves shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The primary contributor to reduction in BK activation at pHO 4.0 over physiologically relevant voltages is the shifted BK gating but not the reduction in single channel conductance.
source: Therefore, the primary contributor to reduction in BK activation at pHO 4.0 over these voltages is the shifted BK gating but not the reduction in single channel conductance.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the comparison of gating shifts and conductance changes.

claim: The gating shift induced by extracellular H+ appeared to be independent of [Ca2+]in.
source: The gating shift induced by extracellular H+ appeared to be independent of [Ca2+]in as a comparable G-V shift was observed with 10 μM [Ca2+]in (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of G-V shifts at different Ca2+ concentrations shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The approximate IC50 of pHO-dependent BK G-V shift is pH 3.8.
source: The approximate IC50 of pHO-dependent BK G-V shift is pH 3.8, suggesting that acidic residue(s) on the extracellular side of the BK channel may be involved in this inhibition.
evidence: This claim is supported by the dose-response curve shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Acidic residue(s) on the extracellular side of the BK channel may be involved in inhibition by extracellular H+.
source: The approximate IC50 of pHO-dependent BK G-V shift is pH 3.8, suggesting that acidic residue(s) on the extracellular side of the BK channel may be involved in this inhibition.
evidence: This is an inference based on the IC50 value being in the range where acidic residues would be protonated.

claim: Extracellular acidification inhibits Kv1 channels by enhancing inactivation in the pore domain.
source: Previous studies suggest that extracellular acidification inhibits Kv1 channels by enhancing inactivation in the pore domain of these channels (Claydon et al., 2007; Kwan et al., 2006; Trapani and Korn, 2003; Zhang et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies on Kv1 channels.

claim: The limiting nPO of BK channels was moderately reduced when pHO was changed from 7 to 4.
source: As shown in Figure 2A and B, the limiting nPO of BK channels was moderately reduced when pHO was changed from 7 to 4.
evidence: This claim is supported by single channel recordings shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: The average limiting nPO of BK channels at pHO 4 was between 0.3 and 0.4 of that at pHO 7.
source: The average limiting nPO of BK channels at pHO 4 was between 0.3 and 0.4 of that at pHOseven among the voltages we tested, indicating that the C-O equilibrium constant L of BK channels at pHO 4 was about 1/3 of that at pHO 7.
evidence: This claim is supported by the quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The C-O equilibrium constant L of BK channels at pHO 4 was about 1/3 of that at pHO 7.
source: The average limiting nPO of BK channels at pHO 4 was between 0.3 and 0.4 of that at pHOseven among the voltages we tested, indicating that the C-O equilibrium constant L of BK channels at pHO 4 was about 1/3 of that at pHO 7.
evidence: This is an inference from the limiting nPO measurements.

claim: G–V curves simulated with L0 scaled to 1/3 of the control value are only predicted to be positively shifted by about 20 mV from the control G-V.
source: As shown in Figures 2C and D, G–V curves simulated with L0 scaled to 1/3 of the control value are only predicted to be positively shifted by about 20 mV from the control G-V, much less than the gating shift observed in our experiments.
evidence: This claim is supported by the H-A model simulations shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: A 1000-fold reduction in L0 was required to reproduce the observed G-V shift if the only effect of extracellular H+ was to alter the C-O equilibrium of BK channel.
source: The H-A simulation also showed that a 1000-fold reduction in L0 was required to reproduce the observed G-V shift if the only effect of extracellular H+ was to alter the C-O equilibrium of BK channel (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the H-A model simulations shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: A change in the C-O equilibrium cannot fully account for the gating shift induced by extracellular acidification.
source: Therefore, a change in the C-O equilibrium cannot fully account for the gating shift induced by extracellular acidification.
evidence: This is an inference from the H-A model simulations showing that the observed C-O equilibrium change is insufficient to explain the full gating shift.

claim: The Vh of BK VSD activation was positively shifted from 190 mV to 309 mV when pHO was changed from 7 to 4.
source: The Boltzmann fit of the Qfast-V relationship shows that the Vh of BK VSD activation was positively shifted from 190 mV to 309 mV when pHO was changed from 7 to 4 (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by gating current measurements and Boltzmann fits shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The slope of Qfast-V relationship was reduced from 0.46e to 0.39e when pHO was changed from 7 to 4.
source: In addition, the slope of Qfast-V relationship was reduced from 0.46e to 0.39e, indicating that the effective gating charge associated with BK VSD movement was moderately reduced by extracellular acidification.
evidence: This claim is supported by the Boltzmann fits of Qfast-V relationships shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The effective gating charge associated with BK VSD movement was moderately reduced by extracellular acidification.
source: In addition, the slope of Qfast-V relationship was reduced from 0.46e to 0.39e, indicating that the effective gating charge associated with BK VSD movement was moderately reduced by extracellular acidification.
evidence: This is an inference from the change in slope of the Qfast-V relationship.

claim: The primary effect of extracellular acidification on BK channels is to inhibit BK VSD activation.
source: Therefore, the primary effect of extracellular acidification on BK channels is to inhibit BK VSD activation.
evidence: This claim is supported by the gating current measurements and H-A model simulations showing that VSD changes account for most of the gating shift.

claim: There are eight acidic residues on the extracellular side of each BK α-subunit.
source: There are eight acidic residues on the extracellular side of each BK α-subunit, with four (D133, E139, D147, D153) in the VSD and the other four (E257, E264, E276, D292) in the PGD (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the structural model shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Four acidic residues (D133, E139, D147, D153) are in the BK VSD.
source: There are eight acidic residues on the extracellular side of each BK α-subunit, with four (D133, E139, D147, D153) in the VSD and the other four (E257, E264, E276, D292) in the PGD (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the structural model shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Four acidic residues (E257, E264, E276, D292) are in the BK PGD.
source: There are eight acidic residues on the extracellular side of each BK α-subunit, with four (D133, E139, D147, D153) in the VSD and the other four (E257, E264, E276, D292) in the PGD (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the structural model shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The acidic residues in the BK VSD are largely conserved among members of the voltage-dependent cation channel superfamily.
source: A multiple sequence alignment in the VSDs of different members of the voltage-dependent cation channel superfamily shows that the acidic residues in the VSD are largely conserved among these channels, with all four residues conserved between BK and Kv channels.
evidence: This claim is supported by the sequence alignment shown in Figure 4B.

claim: All four acidic residues in the BK VSD are conserved between BK and Kv channels.
source: A multiple sequence alignment in the VSDs of different members of the voltage-dependent cation channel superfamily shows that the acidic residues in the VSD are largely conserved among these channels, with all four residues conserved between BK and Kv channels.
evidence: This claim is supported by the sequence alignment shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Only two acidic residues in the pore-loop (E276 and D292) are conserved between BK and Kv channels.
source: For the four acidic residues in the BK PGD, only the two in the pore-loop (E276 and D292) are conserved between BK and Kv channels (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the sequence alignment shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The G-V of hSlo1 D292N is only moderately shifted toward positive potentials when compared with that of WT channels.
source: It should be mentioned that D292, a highly conserved residue among most K channels, has been systemically studied in human BK (hSlo1) channels in a previous study, which showed that the G-V of hSlo1 D292N is only moderately shifted toward positive potentials when compared with that of WT channels (Haug et al., 2004a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a prior study on the D292N mutation.

claim: It is unlikely that the large gating shift of BK channels induced by extracellular acidification would be mainly caused by reduced side chain charge of D292 at low pHO.
source: Therefore, it is unlikely that the large gating shift of BK channels that is induced by extracellular acidification would be mainly caused by reduced side chain charge of D292 at low pHO.
evidence: This is an inference based on the prior study showing modest effects of D292N mutation.

claim: All three alanine substitutions that induced a significant reduction in the pHO-dependent gating shift are in the BK VSD (D133A, D147A, D153A).
source: Consistent with the result that extracellular H+ positively shifts the gating of BK channels mainly by inhibition of BK VSD activation, all three alanine substitutions that induced a significant reduction in the pHO-dependent gating shift are in the BK VSD (D133A, D147A, D153A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the mutagenesis data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Alanine-substitution of D153 had the greatest effect on the pHO-dependent gating shift.
source: Among these three key residues, alanine-substitution of D153 had the greatest effect on the pHO-dependent gating shift.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of the effects of different mutations shown in Figure 5.

claim: The G-V curves of D153A were shifted by less than 10 mV when pHO was changed from 7 to 4.
source: In accordance with this, the G-V curves of D153A were shifted by less than 10 mV when pHO was changed from 7 to 4 (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the G-V curves shown in Figure 5B.

claim: For D153A, the change in gating equilibrium free energy by extracellular acidification at pHO 4 was only 0.3 kcal/mol.
source: Correspondingly, for D153A the change in gating equilibrium free energy by extracellular acidification at pHO 4 (ΔG0pH=G0pH4-G0pH7=zpH4FVhpH4-zpH4FVhpH7) was only 0.3 kcal/mol (Figure 5I).
evidence: This claim is supported by the free energy calculations shown in Figure 5I.

claim: Extracellular acidification increased the gating equilibrium free energy of wild type BK channels by about 2.8 kcal/mol.
source: As a comparison, the same change of pHO increased the gating equilibrium free energy of wild type (WT) BK channels by about 2.8 kcal/mol.
evidence: This claim is supported by the free energy calculations shown in Figure 5I.

claim: D153 is critical for BK inhibition by extracellular H+.
source: This result shows that D153 is critical for BK inhibition by extracellular H+.
evidence: This is an inference from the mutagenesis data showing that D153A nearly abolishes pH sensitivity.

claim: For D133A, changing pHO from 7 to 4 still permitted a G-V shift of about +50 mV.
source: For D133A, changing pHO from 7 to 4 still permitted a G-V shift of about +50 mV (Figure 5C and D), while for D147A, the same extracellular acidification shifted the G-V by more than +60 mV (Figure 5E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by the G-V curves shown in Figure 5C and D.

claim: For D147A, changing pHO from 7 to 4 shifted the G-V by more than +60 mV.
source: For D133A, changing pHO from 7 to 4 still permitted a G-V shift of about +50 mV (Figure 5C and D), while for D147A, the same extracellular acidification shifted the G-V by more than +60 mV (Figure 5E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by the G-V curves shown in Figure 5E and F.

claim: Both D133A and D147A mutations reduced ΔG0pH by more than 1 kcal/mol.
source: Despite the weaker effects of these mutations relative to D153A, both mutations reduced ΔG0pH by more than 1 kcal/mol (Figure 5I), indicating that both aspartates do contribute to BK inhibition by extracellular acidification.
evidence: This claim is supported by the free energy calculations shown in Figure 5I.

claim: Both D133 and D147 contribute to BK inhibition by extracellular acidification.
source: Despite the weaker effects of these mutations relative to D153A, both mutations reduced ΔG0pH by more than 1 kcal/mol (Figure 5I), indicating that both aspartates do contribute to BK inhibition by extracellular acidification.
evidence: This is an inference from the mutagenesis data showing significant effects of these mutations.

claim: The G-V curve of D133A/D147A double mutant was shifted by less than +25 mV when pHO was changed from 7 to 4.
source: Double alanine-substitution of D133 and D147 (D133A/D147A) further reduced the magnitude of the pHO-dependent gating shift. The G-V curve of this double mutant was shifted by less than +25 mV when pHO was changed from 7 to 4 (Figure 5G and H).
evidence: This claim is supported by the G-V curves shown in Figure 5G and H.

claim: The coupling energy between D133 and D147 is 1.2 kcal/mol.
source: The coupling energy between D133 and D147 can be calculated using double-cycle mutation analysis (Yifrach and MacKinnon, 2002) as: [(ΔG0pHWT - ΔG0pHD133A)- (ΔG0pHD147A - ΔG0pHD133AD147A)]=1.2 kcal/mol, indicating that these two acidic residues may not act independently in producing BK inhibition by extracellular acidification.
evidence: This claim is supported by thermodynamic cycle analysis of the mutagenesis data.

claim: D133 and D147 may not act independently in producing BK inhibition by extracellular acidification.
source: The coupling energy between D133 and D147 can be calculated using double-cycle mutation analysis (Yifrach and MacKinnon, 2002) as: [(ΔG0pHWT - ΔG0pHD133A)- (ΔG0pHD147A - ΔG0pHD133AD147A)]=1.2 kcal/mol, indicating that these two acidic residues may not act independently in producing BK inhibition by extracellular acidification.
evidence: This is an inference from the coupling energy calculation.

claim: Alanine-substitution at the three key sites (D133, D147, D153) induced positive gating shifts at pHO 7.
source: By comparing the G-Vs of the above mutants at pHO 7 with that of WT channels it can be noticed that alanine-substitution at these key sites also induced positive gating shifts.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of G-V curves at pH 7 shown in Figure 5.

claim: ΔG0MUT and ΔG0pH are inversely related.
source: From this plot it is clear that ΔG0MUT and ΔG0pH are inversely related, indicating that alanine-substitution of the three key acidic residues and extracellular acidification shift the gating of BK channels by a common mechanism.
evidence: This claim is supported by the correlation plot shown in Figure 5J.

claim: Alanine-substitution of the three key acidic residues and extracellular acidification shift the gating of BK channels by a common mechanism.
source: From this plot it is clear that ΔG0MUT and ΔG0pH are inversely related, indicating that alanine-substitution of the three key acidic residues and extracellular acidification shift the gating of BK channels by a common mechanism.
evidence: This is an inference from the inverse relationship between ΔG0MUT and ΔG0pH.

claim: Inhibition of BK VSD activation is the primary mechanism of BK inhibition by extracellular H+.
source: In this study we describe a strong and reversible inhibitory effect of extracellular H+ on BK channel activation at pHO below 6, with particularly profound effects at pH 5 and 4. This inhibition involves multiple mechanisms, with inhibition of BK VSD activation as the primary mechanism.
evidence: This claim is supported by the gating current measurements and modeling throughout the Results section.

claim: Extracellular H+ induces a moderate change in the C-O equilibrium of channel activation favoring the closed conformation.
source: In addition to inhibition of BK VSD, extracellular H+ also induces a moderate change in the C-O equilibrium of channel activation favoring the closed conformation.
evidence: This claim is supported by the limiting nPO measurements shown in Figure 2.

claim: There is a direct pore inhibition by extracellular protons, but this effect is of minor impact in the face of the large gating shifts.
source: There is also a direct pore inhibition by extracellular protons, but this effect will be of minor impact in the face of the large gating shifts.
evidence: This claim is supported by the single channel conductance measurements shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The combination of effects on VSD activation and C-O equilibrium shifts the G-V relationship of BK toward positive potentials by more than 100 mV at pHO 4.
source: The combination of the effects on VSD activation and C-O equilibrium shifts the G-V relationship of BK toward positive potentials by more than 100 mV at pHO 4.
evidence: This claim is supported by the G-V curves and modeling shown in Figures 1-3.

claim: The activity of BK channels is low in physiological voltage ranges when the channels are exposed to a strongly acidified extracellular environment even with saturating intracellular Ca2+.
source: As a result, the activity of BK channels is low in physiological voltage ranges when the channels are exposed to a strongly acidified extracellular environment even with saturating intracellular Ca2+.
evidence: This claim is supported by the G-V curves at pH 4 shown in Figure 1D.

claim: H+ inhibits BK channel activation mainly by reducing the charge of three acidic residues (D133, D147, D153).
source: We further show that alanine-substitution of three acidic residues in the extracellular side of BK VSD reduces the gating shift caused by extracellular acidification, suggesting that H+ inhibits BK channel activation mainly by reducing the charge of these acidic residues.
evidence: This is an inference from the mutagenesis data showing that neutralizing these residues reduces pH sensitivity.

claim: Inhibition of VSD activation could be a universal mechanism for extracellular H+ to regulate the activity of voltage-dependent ion channels that may be exposed to acidic environments.
source: Since these three acidic residues are highly conserved among voltage-dependent K+ channels, inhibition of VSD activation could be a universal mechanism for extracellular H+ to regulate the activity of voltage-dependent ion channels that may be exposed to acidic environments.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the conservation of key residues and the mechanism identified in BK channels.

claim: Extracellular H+ acts primarily in the pore region of Kv channels at pH above 5.0 to reduce current amplitude.
source: Some previous studies have examined aspects of the effect of extracellular acidification on Kv channels, usually at more moderate pHs above 5.0 (Deutsch and Lee, 1989; Horrigan and Aldrich, 1999a; Claydon et al., 2000; Prole et al., 2003; Kwan et al., 2006; Claydon et al., 2007, Claydon et al., 2008). At such concentrations, extracellular H+ has been observed to act primarily in the pore region of these channels to reduce current amplitude.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies on Kv channels.

claim: pHO 5.9 inhibits Kv 1.5 channels by accelerating entry of open channels into P/C-type inactivation and by stabilizing closed channels in closed-inactivated states.
source: For example, pHO 5.9 inhibits Kv 1.5 channels by accelerating entry of open channels into P/C-type inactivation and by stabilizing closed channels in closed-inactivated states (Claydon et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a prior study on Kv1.5 channels.

claim: Strong acidification at pHs lower than five induces additional inhibition in the BK VSD, most likely by reducing the side chain charges of three key acidic residues.
source: In the current study, we show that strong acidification at pHs lower than five induces additional inhibition in the BK VSD, most likely by reducing the side chain charges of three key acidic residues on the extracellular side of BK VSD.
evidence: This claim is supported by the mutagenesis data and gating current measurements.

claim: The activation of Kv VSD could also be inhibited by strong extracellular acidification.
source: Given that these three residues are highly conserved between BK and Kv channels, it is reasonable to assume that the activation of Kv VSD could also be inhibited by such strong extracellular acidification.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the conservation of key residues between BK and Kv channels.

claim: The G-V and Q-V relationships of Kv1.5 were significantly shifted toward positive potentials at pHO 5 or lower.
source: Indeed, it has been shown that the G-V and Q-V relationships of Kv1.5 were also significantly shifted toward positive potentials at pHO 5 or lower (Claydon et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a prior study on Kv1.5 channels.

claim: D153 in the S2 of BK VSD is the most important residue for BK inhibition by extracellular H+.
source: Among the three key residues involved in BK inhibition by extracellular H+, D153 in the S2 of BK VSD appears to be the most important one as D153A almost completely abolishes the BK gating shift induced by extracellular acidification.
evidence: This claim is supported by the mutagenesis data showing that D153A has the largest effect on pH sensitivity.

claim: D153 was identified as a potential voltage-sensing residue for BK channels by a previous mutagenesis analysis.
source: D153 was identified as a potential voltage-sensing residue for BK channels by a previous mutagenesis analysis of the BK VSD (Ma et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a prior study on BK VSD.

claim: Substitution of D153 by cysteine reduces the zj of BK channels by 40%.
source: In this work the authors analyzed BK ionic current within the framework of the H-A model to show that substitution of D153 by cysteine reduces the zj of BK channels by 40%.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a prior study on the D153C mutation.

claim: The zj of BK channels was reduced by 15% at pHO 4.
source: In agreement with this result, by examining gating currents recorded at different pHOs, we found that the zj of BK channels was reduced by extracellular H+ (Figure 3B). It should be noted that the zj of BK channels was only reduced by 15% at pHO 4, suggesting that the side chain of D153 may still be partially charged at pHO 4.
evidence: This claim is supported by the gating current measurements shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The side chain of D153 may still be partially charged at pHO 4.
source: It should be noted that the zj of BK channels was only reduced by 15% at pHO 4, suggesting that the side chain of D153 may still be partially charged at pHO 4.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that zj is only partially reduced at pH 4.

claim: The BK gating shift induced by changing pHO from 7 to 4 was less than that induced by the D153A mutation.
source: In accordance with this, the BK gating shift induced by changing pHO from 7 to 4 was less than that induced by the D153A mutation (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of G-V curves in Figure 5B.

claim: D153 is located at the bottom of a crevice on the extracellular end of the BK VSD.
source: It can be seen that D153 is located at the bottom of a crevice on the extracellular end of the BK VSD, with little displacement (<1 Å) of D153 between these two structures.
evidence: This claim is supported by the structural models shown in Figure 6A.

claim: There is little displacement (<1 Å) of D153 between the metal-free and liganded mSlo1 structures.
source: It can be seen that D153 is located at the bottom of a crevice on the extracellular end of the BK VSD, with little displacement (<1 Å) of D153 between these two structures.
evidence: This claim is supported by the structural models shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The side chain of R213 is shifted toward the extracellular side by more than 3.5 Å in the liganded structure compared to the metal-free structure.
source: As a comparison, the side chain of R213, another primary voltage sensing residue located in the BK S4 (Ma et al., 2006) is shifted toward the extracellular side by more than 3.5 Å in the liganded structure.
evidence: This claim is supported by the structural models shown in Figure 6A.

claim: In the metal-free structure, one of the carboxyl oxygens in the side chain of D153 is within hydrogen-bonding distance with the δ-nitrogen of R207 (3.1 Å).
source: In the metal-free structure, one of the carboxyl oxygens in the side chain of D153 is within the hydrogen-bonding distance with the δ-nitrogen of R207 (3.1 Å, Figure 6B), while in the liganded structure both carboxyl oxygens of D153 are aligned with the two ω-nitrogens of R210 for potentially strong hydrogen bonding (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the structural analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: In the liganded structure, both carboxyl oxygens of D153 are aligned with the two ω-nitrogens of R210 for potentially strong hydrogen bonding.
source: In the metal-free structure, one of the carboxyl oxygens in the side chain of D153 is within the hydrogen-bonding distance with the δ-nitrogen of R207 (3.1 Å, Figure 6B), while in the liganded structure both carboxyl oxygens of D153 are aligned with the two ω-nitrogens of R210 for potentially strong hydrogen bonding (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the structural analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Both D153 and R207 are required for Cu2+ coordination in the BK VSD in resting states.
source: These observations are in accordance with the result from a previous study of BK inhibition by extracellular Cu2+, which shows that both D153 and R207 are required for Cu2+ coordination in the BK VSD in resting states (Ma et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a prior study on Cu2+ inhibition of BK channels.

claim: D153 might interact with various basic residues in BK S4 to stabilize the VSD in particular transitional conformations on the pathway to activation.
source: Thus, it is conceivable that D153 might interact with various basic residues in BK S4 to stabilize the VSD in particular transitional conformations on the pathway to activation.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the structural observations and prior studies.

claim: Extracellular acidification could inhibit BK VSD activation by weakening interactions between D153 and S4 basic residues.
source: If this was true, then extracellular acidification could inhibit BK VSD activation by weakening such interactions.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the proposed mechanism of D153 function.

claim: Residues with opposite charges placed at Shaker 283 and Shaker 368 can stabilize the VSD of the resulting Shaker channel in a partially active conformation.
source: Indeed, previous work shows that residues with opposite charges placed at Shaker 283 and Shaker 368 (homologous to mSlo1 R210) can stabilize the VSD of the resulting Shaker channel in a partially active conformation (Tiwari-Woodruff et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a prior study on Shaker channels.

claim: D133 and D147 are more exposed to the extracellular environment than D153 in both mSlo1 structures.
source: D133 and D147 are more exposed to the extracellular environment than D153 in both mSlo1 structures (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the structural models shown in Figure 6A.

claim: There is little change in position of D133 between the metal-free and liganded structures.
source: For D133 in the S1 helix of BK VSD, there is little change in position between the two structures.
evidence: This claim is supported by the structural models shown in Figure 6.

claim: The side chain of D133 is close to R207 in both mSlo1 structures.
source: The side chain of D133 is close to R207 in both mSlo1 structures (Figure 6D–E), indicating that D133 may also form important interactions with S4 residues to stabilize BK VSD.
evidence: This claim is supported by the structural analysis shown in Figure 6D-E.

claim: D133 may form important interactions with S4 residues to stabilize BK VSD.
source: The side chain of D133 is close to R207 in both mSlo1 structures (Figure 6D–E), indicating that D133 may also form important interactions with S4 residues to stabilize BK VSD.
evidence: This is an inference from the structural proximity of D133 and R207.

claim: D133 is involved in Cu2+ coordination with the BK VSD.
source: Interestingly, D133 is also involved in Cu2+ coordination with the BK VSD (Ma et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a prior study on Cu2+ inhibition of BK channels.

claim: Either the state-dependence of Cu2+-VSD coordination is largely determined by the distance between D153 and R207, or the conformation captured by the liganded structure represents a partially activated VSD state.
source: The lack of change in distance between D133 and R207 in the two mSlo1 structures indicates that either the state-dependence of Cu2+-VSD coordination is largely determined by the distance between D153 and R207, or the conformation captured by the liganded structure represents a partially activated VSD state.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the structural observations and prior Cu2+ coordination studies.

claim: D147 undergoes a large displacement between the metal-free and liganded structures.
source: For D147, a large displacement is observed between the two structures, which is not totally unexpected as D147 is in the flexible S1-S2 linker.
evidence: This claim is supported by the structural models.

claim: The displacement of D147 is largely horizontal.
source: However, this displacement is largely horizontal. Thus, D147 remains on the surface of the BK VSD in both structures.
evidence: This claim is supported by the structural models.

claim: D147 remains on the surface of the BK VSD in both structures.
source: However, this displacement is largely horizontal. Thus, D147 remains on the surface of the BK VSD in both structures.
evidence: This claim is supported by the structural models.

claim: The side chain of D147 is not close to any residue with potential for strong interaction in the two mSlo1 structures.
source: Unlike that of D153 and D133, the side chain of D147 is not close to any residue with potential for strong interaction in the two mSlo1 structure, indicating that D147 may not contribute to VSD activation by interacting with other residues to stabilize transitional conformations during VSD activation.
evidence: This claim is supported by the structural analysis.

claim: D147 may not contribute to VSD activation by interacting with other residues to stabilize transitional conformations during VSD activation.
source: Unlike that of D153 and D133, the side chain of D147 is not close to any residue with potential for strong interaction in the two mSlo1 structure, indicating that D147 may not contribute to VSD activation by interacting with other residues to stabilize transitional conformations during VSD activation.
evidence: This is an inference from the structural observations.

claim: D147 may participate in BK VSD activation by altering local electric field.
source: Instead, D147 may participate in BK VSD activation by altering local electric field.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the structural observations.

claim: D133 and D153 are highly conserved among the members of the voltage-dependent cation channel superfamily.
source: The sequence alignment in Figure 4B shows that D133 and D153 are highly conserved among the members of the voltage-dependent cation channel superfamily.
evidence: This claim is supported by the sequence alignment shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Acidic residues D133 and D153 may form critical interactions with S4 basic residues during the activation of Kv channels.
source: Previous studies (Long et al., 2007; Pathak et al., 2007; Tao et al., 2010; Hoshi and Armstrong, 2012) suggest that these acidic residues may form critical interactions with S4 basic residues during the activation of Kv channels.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies on Kv channels.

claim: Extracellularly applied La3+ interacts with Kv1.2 E183 and E226 to inhibit the activation of Kv VSD.
source: For example, it has been reported that extracellularly applied La3+ interacts with Kv1.2 E183 and E226 (homologous to mSlo1 D133 and D153, respectively) to inhibit the activation of Kv VSD (Hoshi and Armstrong, 2012), a mechanism that may underlie the inhibitory effect of extracellular divalent cations observed in Kv (Gilly and Armstrong, 1982; Zhang et al., 2001a) and Nav (Frankenhaeuser and Hodgkin, 1957; Hille et al., 1975) channels.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a prior study on La3+ inhibition of Kv channels.

claim: Extracellular H+ may inhibit the activation of members in the voltage-dependent cation channel superfamily by a mechanism similar to that in BK channels.
source: Therefore, it is reasonable to assume that extracellular H+ may also inhibit the activation of members in the voltage-dependent cation channel superfamily by a similar mechanism.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the conservation of key residues and mechanisms.

claim: The D153A mutation alone can almost completely abolish the gating shift induced by extracellular acidification.
source: In the current study we found that the D153A mutation alone can almost completely abolish the gating shift induced by extracellular acidification.
evidence: This claim is supported by the mutagenesis data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The shallow slope of the pHO-dependent gating-shift curve indicates that multiple sites with different pKa values may be involved in BK inhibition by extracellular H+.
source: However, the shallow slope of the pHO-dependent gating-shift curve shown in Figure 1E indicates that multiple sites with different pKa values may be involved in BK inhibition by extracellular H+.
evidence: This is an inference from the dose-response curve shape.

claim: The pKa of Asp and Glu can differ substantially from the expected value of around 4, depending on aqueous exposure and interaction with nearby charged residues.
source: Previous studies show that, depending on aqueous exposure and interaction with nearby charged residues, the pKa of Asp and Glu can differ substantially from the expected value of around 4 (Forsyth et al., 2002; Ma et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies on pKa values of acidic residues.

claim: The three acidic residues identified in this study may be exposed to different local environments that result in somewhat modified pKa values.
source: Therefore, it is possible that the three acidic residues identified in this study may be exposed to different local environments that result in somewhat modified pKa values.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on known properties of acidic residues in proteins.

claim: Another extracellular residue with higher pKa may be involved in BK regulation by extracellular H+.
source: It is also possible that another extracellular residue with higher pKa is involved in BK regulation by extracellular H+.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the shallow dose-response curve.

claim: mSlo1 H254 in the S5 of BK PGD is a possible candidate for an additional pHO sensor.
source: One possible candidate for an additional pHO sensor is mSlo1 H254 in the S5 of BK PGD.
evidence: This is a speculative claim suggesting a potential additional pH sensor.

claim: Regulation of BK channels by cytosolic factors has been extensively studied.
source: Whereas regulation of BK channels by cytosolic factors has been extensively studied (Hou et al., 2009), much less is known about how physiological signals may regulate BK channels on the extracellular face of the BK channel.
evidence: This claim reflects the state of knowledge in the field, supported by a citation.

claim: BK channels are ubiquitously expressed in lysosomal membranes in both excitable and non-excitable cells.
source: Two recent studies suggest that BK channels are ubiquitously expressed in lysosomal membranes in both excitable and non-excitable cells (Cao et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent studies on lysosomal BK channels.

claim: Lysosomal BK channels are functionally coupled with the lysosomal Ca2+-permeable channel TRPML1 to regulate lysosomal Ca2+ release/refilling.
source: The results from these studies suggest that lysosomal BK channels are functionally coupled with the lysosomal Ca2+-permeable channel TRPML1 to regulate lysosomal Ca2+ release/refilling, which is a key process underlying lysosomal physiology (Xu and Ren, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on lysosomal BK channels and Ca2+ regulation.

claim: Lysosomal Ca2+ release/refilling is a key process underlying lysosomal physiology.
source: The results from these studies suggest that lysosomal BK channels are functionally coupled with the lysosomal Ca2+-permeable channel TRPML1 to regulate lysosomal Ca2+ release/refilling, which is a key process underlying lysosomal physiology (Xu and Ren, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a review on lysosomal physiology.

claim: The extracellular side of the lysosomal BK channel is expected to be exposed to the acidic environment of the lysosome lumen.
source: Since the extracellular side of the lysosomal BK channel is expected to be exposed to the acidic environment of the lysosome lumen, the basal activity of the lysosomal BK channel is expected to be low.
evidence: This is an inference based on the orientation of BK channels in lysosomal membranes and the known acidic pH of lysosomes.

claim: The basal activity of the lysosomal BK channel is expected to be low.
source: Since the extracellular side of the lysosomal BK channel is expected to be exposed to the acidic environment of the lysosome lumen, the basal activity of the lysosomal BK channel is expected to be low.
evidence: This is an inference based on the findings of this study showing that low pH inhibits BK channels.

claim: Lysosomal pH is highly heterogeneous, with the luminal pH of some primary lysosomes close to 7.
source: However, it should be noted that lysosomal pH is highly heterogeneous, with the luminal pH of some primary lysosomes close to 7 (Johnson et al., 2016; Bright et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on lysosomal pH heterogeneity.

claim: The activity of lysosomal BK channels might be regulated by lysosomal luminal pH.
source: Therefore, it is conceivable that the activity of lysosomal BK channels might be regulated by lysosomal luminal pH.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the pH sensitivity of BK channels and the heterogeneity of lysosomal pH.

claim: BK channels are sensitive to intracellular H+, which mimics the effect of Ca2+-binding in the BK RCK1 domain.
source: Interestingly, BK channels are also sensitive to intracellular H+, which mimics the effect of Ca2+-binding in the BK RCK1 domain (Avdonin et al., 2003; Hou et al., 2008a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies on intracellular pH effects on BK channels.

claim: Intracellular H+ may enhance the activity of BK channels in the absence of intracellular Ca2+.
source: Thus, intracellular H+ may enhance the activity of BK channels in the absence of intracellular Ca2+, while during elevations of intracellular Ca2+, intracellular H+ may inhibit BK channel activity (Cook et al., 1984; Christensen and Zeuthen, 1987; Schubert et al., 2001; Guarina et al., 2017), presumably by interfering with Ca2+-binding.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies on intracellular pH effects on BK channels.

claim: During elevations of intracellular Ca2+, intracellular H+ may inhibit BK channel activity, presumably by interfering with Ca2+-binding.
source: Thus, intracellular H+ may enhance the activity of BK channels in the absence of intracellular Ca2+, while during elevations of intracellular Ca2+, intracellular H+ may inhibit BK channel activity (Cook et al., 1984; Christensen and Zeuthen, 1987; Schubert et al., 2001; Guarina et al., 2017), presumably by interfering with Ca2+-binding.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies, with the mechanism being speculative.

claim: Any consideration of the role of BK channels in lysosomes must take into account its regulation by luminal pH.
source: In any case, it is clear that the present results require that any consideration of the role of BK channels in lysosomes must take into account its regulation by luminal pH.
evidence: This is an inference from the findings of this study.

claim: BK channels in mouse chromaffin cells are inhibited by extracellular H+.
source: Although it seems unlikely that neurons will be exposed to pH as low as those required to inhibit BK channels in the presence study, a recent study has observed that BK channels in mouse chromaffin cells (MCC) are inhibited by extracellular H+ (Guarina et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a recent study on chromaffin cells.

claim: The IC50 of MCC BK inhibition by extracellular H+ is 0.1 μM (pH 7).
source: The mechanism underlying this inhibition appears to be different from that described in the current study for two reasons: first, the IC50 of MCC BK inhibition by extracellular H+ is 0.1 μM (pH 7), which is lower than what we observed in our experiment (52 μM/pH 4.3).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a study on chromaffin cells.

claim: The onset (>30 s) and recovery (~3 min) of MCC BK inhibition by extracellular H+ is much slower than that of the inhibition described in this study (<1 s for both onset and recovery).
source: Second, the onset (>30 s) and recovery (~3 min) of MCC BK inhibition by extracellular H+ is much slower than that of the inhibition described here (<1 s for both onset and recovery).
evidence: This claim compares the kinetics observed in this study with those reported in a prior study on chromaffin cells.

claim: At least some of the BK inhibition observed in chromaffin cells with extracellular acidification may reflect the time course of intracellular acidification induced from elevation of extracellular [H+].
source: Based on the IC50 and the time course of MCC BK inhibition by extracellular H+, it seems likely that at least some of the BK inhibition observed in CCs with extracellular acidification may reflect the time course of intracellular acidification induced from elevation of extracellular [H+].
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on comparison of the mechanisms and kinetics.
